q1000.q: Which muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve?
q1000.ex: The ulnar nerve is the primary motor nerve of the hand, responsible for fine motor control. It innervates all the intrinsic muscles of the hand except for the three thenar muscles (Abductor Pollicis Brevis, Flexor Pollicis Brevis, Opponens Pollicis) and the lateral two lumbricals (1st and 2nd), which are supplied by the median nerve. Let's analyze the options: (A) The Dorsal interossei (DAB) are responsible for finger abduction and are all supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. (B) The Abductor digiti minimi is a key muscle of the hypothenar eminence, which is entirely supplied by the ulnar nerve. (C) The 4th lumbrical (along with the 3rd) is one of the two medial lumbricals, which are supplied by the ulnar nerve, in contrast to the 1st and 2nd lumbricals (supplied by the median nerve). Since the ulnar nerve supplies all three of these structures, the correct answer is (D) All of the above. 2. What is the function of the muscle that attaches to the indicated area? (A)	Protraction (B) Retraction (C)	Depression (D)	Elevation EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025 (C) Depression The image indicates the gluteus medius muscle, which arises from the outer surface of the ilium and inserts into the greater trochanter of the femur. The gluteus medius is one of the principal muscles of the hip and plays a crucial role in maintaining pelvic stability during locomotion. The primary function of the gluteus medius is abduction of the thigh at the hip joint. In addition, it is responsible for stabilizing the pelvis during walking or standing on one leg. When one foot is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius on the opposite side contracts to prevent the pelvis from tilting downward. This action is essential for maintaining balance and proper gait. Weakness of this muscle results in a positive Trendelenburg sign. The muscle does not primarily produce protraction or retraction, which are movements associated with the scapula. It also does not cause elevation in this context. While it contributes to hip abduction and medial rotation, among the given options, the closest related movement affecting pelvic mechanics is depression, referring to stabilization and prevention of pelvic drop. Therefore, the correct answer is : (C) Depression 3. Which nerve is not related to olfaction? (A)	Hypoglossal (B) Trigeminal (C)	Glossopharyngeal (D)	Vagus EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025 (A) Hypoglossal Olfaction (the sense of smell) is a complex sensation. While the olfactory nerve (CN I) is the primary nerve for detecting odorants, other nerves contribute to the overall perception. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) (B) is related because it provides general sensation from the nasal mucosa, detecting chemical irritants or qualities like the "cooling" of menthol or the "burn" of ammonia (chemosensation). The glossopharyngeal (CN IX) (C) and vagus (CN X) (D) nerves are related because they mediate taste from the posterior tongue and pharynx. The perception of "flavor" is a combined sensory experience that intimately links retronasal olfaction with taste. In contrast, the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) (A) is a purely motor nerve. It supplies the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (except palatoglossus), controlling tongue movement. It has no sensory function related to smell, taste, or flavor perception. 4. What is the nerve supply to the piriform fossa? (A)	Internal laryngeal nerve (B) Recurrent laryngeal nerve (C)	External laryngeal nerve (D)	Glossopharyngeal nerve EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025 (A) Internal laryngeal nerve The piriform fossa (or recess) is a depression in the laryngopharynx located on either side of the laryngeal inlet. The sensory innervation of the larynx is divided by the vocal cords. The mucosa above the vocal cords, which includes the piriform fossa, is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve (A). This nerve is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which arises from the vagus (CN X). This innervation is critical as it provides the sensory (afferent) limb of the cough reflex for this area. (B) The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the mucosa below the vocal cords. (C) The external laryngeal nerve is a motor nerve that supplies the cricothyroid muscle. (D) The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies sensation to the oropharynx (e.g., tonsils, posterior tongue), which is superior to the piriform fossa. 5. A 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department complaining that food is stuck in his throat. Examination reveals a bone lodged in the left piriform recess. Which function is most likely to be affected? (A)	Cough reflex (B) Gag reflex (C)	Mastication (D)	Salivation EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025 (A) Cough reflex This clinical scenario is a direct application of the anatomy from the previous question. The piriform recess is innervated by the internal laryngeal nerve. This nerve provides the sensory afferent limb for the cough reflex (A) for any foreign material at or above the laryngeal inlet. A foreign body, such as a fishbone, lodged in this recess can mechanically or by local inflammation/edema, "anesthetize" the nerve endings. This impairs the protective reflex, which normally detects the foreign body and triggers a cough to expel it. This impairment significantly increases the risk of aspiration. The gag reflex (B) is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) in the oropharynx, a different location. These muscles originate from the ilium and insert on the greater trochanter of the femur. Their primary and most powerful action is hip abduction (B), which is the movement of the thigh away from the body's midline. These muscles are the main abductors of the hip. They also play a crucial role in pelvic stability. When standing on one leg, the gluteus medius and minimus on the standing side contract isometrically to prevent the pelvis from dropping on the opposite (swinging) side, a function tested by the Trendelenburg test. While the anterior fibers of these muscles can assist in internal rotation (A), their main function is abduction. Knee extension (C) and knee flexion (D) are actions at the knee joint, controlled by the quadriceps and hamstrings, respectively. 7. Which of the following is not a boundary of the hepatocystic triangle? (A)	Common hepatic duct (B) Cystic duct (C)	Right lobe of liver (D)	Cystic artery EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025 (D) Cystic artery The hepatocystic triangle, also known as the Triangle of Calot, is a critical anatomical space for surgeons, especially during a cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal). Which muscles are supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve? (A)	Peroneus longus & Brevis (B) Extensor hallucis longus (C)	Peroneus tertius (D)	Both A & C EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025 (A) Peroneus longus & Brevis The common peroneal (fibular) nerve divides into two main branches: the superficial and deep peroneal nerves. 1. The superficial peroneal nerve (also called the superficial fibular nerve) supplies the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg. These muscles are the Peroneus longus and Peroneus brevis (A). Their primary function is eversion of the foot, and they also assist in plantarflexion. 2. The deep peroneal nerve (deep fibular nerve) supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg. q1032.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with easy bruising and petechiae, a platelet count of 18,000/mm³, normal hemoglobin and leukocyte counts, and a recent mild upper respiratory infection. Her peripheral smear is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
q1032.ex: This patient has isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet count 18,000/mm³) with normal hemoglobin and leukocyte counts, a normal peripheral smear, and a recent viral infection. This presentation is classic for immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), an autoimmune condition in which antibodies (usually IgG) target platelets, leading to their destruction in the spleen. In adults with symptomatic ITP or platelet count below 30,000/mm³, the first-line treatment is corticosteroids (such as oral prednisone or dexamethasone). Steroids reduce antibody production and decrease splenic clearance of platelets. Platelet transfusion is reserved for severe or life-threatening bleeding, as transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed. Bone marrow biopsy is not routinely required when the clinical picture clearly suggests ITP. Splenectomy is considered a second-line therapy for chronic or steroid-refractory cases. Therefore, the most appropriate next step is oral corticosteroids. NODIA 11===

q1049.q: Which of the following is not true regarding bempedoic acid?
o: It non-competitively inhibits ATP citrate lyase
It is used when statins and diet cannot control dyslipidemia
It inhibits de-novo synthesis of liver cholesterol
q1049.ex: Bempedoic acid is a newer, non-statin agent used for lowering LDL cholesterol. It is a prodrug that is activated in the liver. Its mechanism (D) is to inhibit de novo cholesterol synthesis at a step upstream of statins. It blocks ATP citrate lyase (ACL), the enzyme that converts citrate to acetyl-CoA in the cytoplasm, thereby reducing the acetyl-CoA pool available for cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis. This inhibition is competitive with its substrate, citrate, not non-competitive (B). Statement (C) is its correct clinical indication: it is used as an adjunct to diet and maximally tolerated statin therapy for patients who need further LDL-C reduction. While it is technically a prodrug, its active form, bempedoyl-CoA, works, and the parent molecule (A) is indeed a dicarboxylic acid. Therefore, the incorrect statement is (B) because the inhibition of ACL is competitive. NODIA 13===

q1069.q: In a suspected poisoning case, gastric lavage fluid turns black when mixed with silver nitrate solution. This occurs in which type of poisoning?
q1069.ex: Aluminium phosphide (A) is a toxic pesticide that reacts with water in the stomach to produce phosphine gas (PH3). This phosphine gas is a potent reducing agent. When the gastric lavage fluid (containing the dissolved phosphine) is mixed with a silver nitrate solution, the phosphine reduces the silver ions (Ag+) to metallic silver (Ag). Metallic silver is black, so the solution turns black, or a black precipitate forms. This is a classic diagnostic bedside test for aluminium phosphide poisoning. This reaction does not occur with organophosphorus compounds (B), opium (C), or cocaine (D).

q1082.q: According to NACO guidelines, which of the following does not fall under the High-Risk Groups for HIV?
q1082.ex: India's National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) focuses its interventions on specific populations with the highest risk of HIV transmission. These are termed "High-Risk Groups" (HRGs). The core HRGs are: 1. Female Sex Workers (FSW) (B) 2. Men who have sex with Men (MSM) (A) 3. Injecting Drug Users (IDUs) (D) 4. Transgender (TG) / Hijras Truck drivers (C) are not classified as an HRG. They are classified as a "Bridge Population." A bridge population is one that has links to both high-risk groups (e.g., they may be clients of FSWs) and the low-risk "general population" (their regular partners). While they are a critical group for HIV intervention, they are not in the same core high-risk category as FSW, MSM, and IDUs.

q1111.q: The murmur of mitral stenosis corresponds to which ECG wave?
q1111.ex: The murmur of mitral stenosis is a low-pitched, rumbling mid-diastolic murmur. In patients who are in sinus rhythm, this murmur often has a pre-systolic accentuation (it gets louder just before the first heart sound). This late-diastolic, crescendo component of the murmur is caused by the contraction of the left atrium, which actively pushes a final bolus of blood through the narrowed mitral valve. The electrical event on the ECG that represents atrial contraction (atrial depolarization) is the P wave. Therefore, the pre-systolic accentuation of the mitral stenosis murmur follows the P wave and corresponds to the atrial "kick."

q1170.q: In a patient with septic shock who stays hypotensive even after adequate fluid resuscitation, what should be the next medication of choice?
q1170.ex: The patient is in fluid-refractory septic shock, as defined by persistent hypotension (low MAP) despite "adequate fluid resuscitation." The immediate goal is to restore tissue perfusion by increasing the mean arterial pressure (MAP) to a target of mmHg. This requires the initiation of a vasopressor. According to the international Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines, the first-line vasopressor of choice is noradrenaline (norepinephrine) (A). It is favored for its potent alpha-adrenergic effects, which cause peripheral vasoconstriction and increase blood pressure, with less of the arrhythmogenic beta-adrenergic effects seen with other agents. Adrenaline (B) is typically added as a second-line agent if noradrenaline alone is insufficient. Dopamine (C) is no longer a first-line choice due to its higher risk of arrhythmias. Hydrocortisone (D) is an adjuvant therapy given in refractory shock, not the primary vasopressor.

q1185.q: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Alcohol in low dose causes brain stimulation and in higher doses, causes brain suppression
Cannabis use can result in self-driven, repetitive behaviours
Opioids are very effective analgesics NODIA
Volatile inhalational agents are mostly toxic to humans
q1185.ex: This statement is incorrect from a pharmacological perspective. Alcohol is a central nervous system (CNS) depressant at all doses. The "stimulation" (e.g., euphoria, talkativeness, disinhibition) felt at low doses is not true stimulation (like that from amphetamines). It is a "pseudo-stimulation" caused by the depression or disinhibition of higher cortical centers in the brain (like the prefrontal cortex) that normally govern social control and judgment. As the dose increases, the depressant effects become more pronounced, leading to sedation, ataxia, and eventual "brain suppression." Therefore, alcohol never truly "causes brain stimulation." The other statements are considered correct in this context. (C) Opioids are a gold standard for analgesia. (D) Volatile inhalational agents in the context of substance abuse (e.g., solvents, glue) are mostly toxic. (B) Cannabis use can be associated with repetitive behaviors.

q1187.q: What is the role of the secretions produced by the region indicated by the arrow in the given histology image?
q1187.ex: The provided histology image shows a cross-section of the adrenal gland. The arrow is pointing to the zona glomerulosa, the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex. This zone is responsible for synthesizing and secreting mineralocorticoids, with aldosterone being the most significant. The primary function of aldosterone is the regulation of blood pressure and electrolyte balance. It acts on the distal tubules and collecting ducts of the kidneys to increase the reabsorption of sodium and water, and to enhance the excretion of potassium. Sexual function (Option A) is primarily influenced by androgens secreted from the zona reticularis. Maintenance of glucose levels (Option B) is a key function of glucocorticoids, such as cortisol, which are secreted by the zona fasciculata. The emergency "fight-or-flight" response (Option D) is mediated by catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) secreted by the adrenal medulla, not the cortex. 2. Which type of joint is NOT associated with the bone illustrated in the diagram? (A)	Syndesmosis (B) Symphysis (C)	Plane synovial joint (D)	Synchondrosis EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024 (D) Synchondrosis The bone shown in the image is a rib, identifiable by its elongated, curved shape and posterior articulation features. Ribs are associated with the following joint types: 1. Plane synovial joints (C) → At the costovertebral and costotransverse joints between the rib and vertebrae. 2. Syndesmosis (A) → The interosseous ligaments between rib and vertebrae contribute to fibrous union. 3. Symphysis (B) → Indirectly associated via the manubriosternal joint (sternal angle) and some costal cartilage interactions. However, a synchondrosis (D) is a primary cartilaginous joint where bones are united by hyaline cartilage, such as the epiphyseal plate or first sternocostal joint (sometimes classified differently). Ribs themselves do not form true synchondroses directly in typical articulation patterns, except in early developmental stages. Thus, among the options listed, the joint type not typically associated with the rib is : (D) Synchondrosis. 3. The spinal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve sends its second-order neurons to transmit which type of sensation? (A)	Touch (B) Pain (C)	Vibration (D)	Proprioception EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024 (B) Pain The sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve in the brainstem is divided into three parts. The principal (or chief) sensory nucleus processes discriminative touch and pressure. The mesencephalic nucleus handles proprioception from the muscles of mastication. The spinal sensory nucleus is primarily responsible for processing protopathic sensations, which include pain and temperature, as well as crude touch from the ipsilateral side of the face. First-order neurons from the trigeminal ganglion synapse in the spinal nucleus. The second-order neurons then decussate (cross the midline) and ascend in the ventral two-dimensionality tract to the contralateral thalamus (VPM nucleus). From there, third-order neurons project to the somatosensory cortex. Fine touch (Option A) is primarily handled by the principal nucleus, while vibration (Option C) and proprioception (Option D) are carried by other pathways. 4. The substantia nigra has functional connections with which component of the basal ganglia? (A)	Striatum (B) Pallidum (C)	Subthalamic nucleus (D)	Thalamus EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024 (A) Striatum The substantia nigra, located in the midbrain, is a crucial component of the basal ganglia motor circuitry. It is most famously and extensively connected to the striatum (which consists of the caudate nucleus and the putamen). This connection forms the nigrostriatal pathway, where dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) project to the striatum to modulate its activity. This pathway is essential for the initiation and smooth execution of voluntary movements, and its degeneration is the primary pathology in Parkinson's disease. While the substantia nigra pars reticulata receives input from the striatum and projects to the thalamus (Option D), its most prominent functional connection is its dopaminergic input to the striatum. The pallidum (Option B) and subthalamic nucleus (Option C) are other key nodes within the basal ganglia circuit but are not the primary connection site for the substantia nigra. 5. Which structure is NOT present in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle? (A)	Hippocampus (B) Tail of the caudate nucleus (C)	Fimbria (D)	Collateral eminence EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2024 (B) Tail of the caudate nucleus The inferior (temporal) horn of the lateral ventricle extends into the temporal lobe. Its floor is a complex surface formed by several structures. These include the hippocampus (Option A), a key structure for memory formation, which creates a prominent bulge in the floor. The fimbria of the hippocampus (Option C), a band of efferent fibers, runs along its medial edge. The most lateral part of the floor is the collateral eminence (Option D), a ridge formed by the underlying collateral sulcus. In contrast, the tail of the caudate nucleus is a component of the roof of the inferior horn. It arches over the thalamus and follows the curve of the lateral ventricle, terminating anteriorly at the amygdala. Therefore, it is not found in the floor of the inferior horn. 6. q1191.ex: The correct answer is (A) 1. SST, 2. GHRH, 3. GH, 4. IGF, which represents the normal physiological regulation of growth hormone secretion through the hypothalamic–pituitary–liver axis. Growth hormone (GH) secretion is controlled by two hormones released from the hypothalamus. The first is Somatostatin (SST), which acts as an inhibitory hormone. It suppresses the secretion of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary gland. The second hormone is Growth Hormone Releasing Hormone (GHRH), which stimulates the somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary to release growth hormone. Once released, Growth Hormone (GH) enters the bloodstream and acts on various tissues. One of its most important actions is stimulating the liver to produce Insulin-like Growth Factor (IGF-1). IGF-1 mediates most of the growth-promoting effects of GH, including bone growth, protein synthesis, and cell proliferation. IGF-1 also exerts negative feedback on both the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. It decreases GHRH secretion and increases somatostatin release, thereby regulating GH levels. Thus, option (A) correctly represents this hormonal regulatory pathway.

q1217.q: All of the following are growth-promoting proto-oncogenes except?
q1217.ex: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that, when mutated or overexpressed, can contribute to cancer formation. Many code for growth factors or their receptors. Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF, A), Platelet-Derived Growth Factor (PDGF, B), and Transforming Growth Factor-alpha (TGF-alpha, C) are all potent growth factors whose genes function as proto-oncogenes; their overexpression can drive cell proliferation. In contrast, Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-beta) has a complex, context-dependent role but is primarily considered a tumor suppressor. It inhibits the proliferation of many cell types, including epithelial cells, and promotes apoptosis. Loss-of-function mutations in the TGF-beta signaling pathway are common in many cancers, allowing cells to escape its growth-inhibitory effects. Therefore, TGF-beta is not a growth-promoting proto-oncogene.

q1279.q: All of the following are seen in third nerve (oculomotor nerve) palsy except:
q1279.ex: The third cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve) innervates the levator palpebrae superioris, the pupillary sphincter, and four extraocular muscles: the superior, inferior, and medial recti, and the inferior oblique. A complete palsy of this nerve results in ptosis (drooping eyelid) (A) due to paralysis of the levator muscle. It also causes a fixed, dilated pupil (mydriasis) (B) because of the unopposed action of the sympathetic nervous system. The eye deviates "down and out" due to the unopposed action of the lateral rectus (innervated by CN VI) and superior oblique (innervated by CN IV) muscles, resulting in a combination of exotropia (outward deviation) and hypotropia (downward deviation) (D). Abduction (outward movement of the eye) is the primary function of the lateral rectus muscle, which is innervated by the sixth cranial nerve (abducens nerve). Therefore, loss of abduction is not seen in a third nerve palsy; in fact, abduction is unopposed.

q1297.q: Which of the following is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST)? NODIA 94===
q1297.ex: Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs) are mesenchymal neoplasms defined by specific molecular markers. The vast majority (~95%) are positive for the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT (CD117) (B). A subset of KIT-negative GISTs have mutations in the related receptor PDGFRA (C). A small percentage of GISTs lacking KIT or PDGFRA mutations (wild-type GISTs) have defects in the succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) enzyme complex (A). These three markers are key to the diagnosis and classification of GISTs. Nestin (D), however, is an intermediate filament protein that serves as a marker for neural stem cells and progenitor cells. While it can be expressed in some other tumors, it is not a characteristic or diagnostic marker for GISTs.

q1310.q: The Mount Fuji sign on CT is seen in which of the following conditions?
q1310.ex: The Mount Fuji sign is a specific radiological sign seen on a non-contrast CT scan of the head in patients with tension pneumocephalus. Pneumocephalus is the presence of air or gas within the cranial cavity. In tension pneumocephalus, the trapped intracranial air exerts mass effect. The Mount Fuji sign describes the appearance of bilateral subdural air collections that compress both frontal lobes, causing them to separate and collapse, resembling the silhouette of Mount Fuji in Japan. This is a neurosurgical emergency that requires prompt intervention to decompress the trapped air. This sign is specific to the intracranial space and is not seen in pneumoperitoneum (B), pneumomediastinum (C), or pneumothorax (D).

q1325.q: A newborn presents with frothy oral secretions and respiratory distress. An X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis? NODIA 98===
q1325.ex: The clinical presentation of a newborn with excessive frothiness from the mouth, choking, and respiratory distress is highly suggestive of esophageal atresia (EA), which is almost always associated with a tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). The provided chest X-ray is diagnostic. It shows the nasogastric (or orogastric) tube failing to pass into the stomach and instead coiling in the blind-ending upper esophageal pouch. This finding confirms the diagnosis of esophageal atresia. The presence of gas in the stomach and intestines on the X-ray indicates the most common type, which is EA with a distal TEF. The other conditions have different clinical and radiological presentations (e.g., fluid in the fissure for TTN, ground-glass opacities for HMD, bowel loops in the chest for Bochdalek hernia).

q1352.q: A 28-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks comes for a routine prenatal checkup. During the ultrasound, several measurements are taken to assess fetal growth. Which of the following is not used as a criterion for diagnosing intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)?
o: Fetal weight less than the 3rd percentile (-3 SD)
Uterine artery pulsatility index (PI) greater than 95th percentile NODIA
Abdominal circumference (AC) less than the 3rd percentile (-3 SD)
q1352.ex: IUGR is diagnosed when the fetus fails to achieve its genetically predetermined growth potential. Diagnostic ultrasound parameters include fetal weight and abdominal circumference below the 10th percentile (or 3rd percentile for severe IUGR), and Doppler studies such as absent or reversed end-diastolic flow (AEDF/REDF) in the umbilical artery. While increased uterine artery PI indicates high placental resistance and predicts the risk of IUGR, it is not a diagnostic criterion itself. Instead, it serves as an ancillary marker suggesting uteroplacental insufficiency. The combination of biometric and Doppler findings provides a comprehensive assessment of fetal health. Management involves close monitoring, optimizing maternal nutrition, and timely delivery if fetal compromise develops. Early detection and differentiation between symmetrical and asymmetrical IUGR are crucial, as the latter (due to placental insufficiency) is more common and amenable to intervention. Accurate diagnosis minimizes perinatal morbidity and mortality through appropriate timing of delivery and neonatal care.

q1377.q: What deficit results from an injury to the posterior interosseous nerve?
q1377.ex: The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is the deep, purely motor branch of the radial nerve. It innervates the muscles in the extensor compartment of the forearm. A crucial anatomical point is that the radial nerve gives off branches to the main wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis) before the PIN is formed. Therefore, in an isolated PIN palsy, wrist extension is largely preserved, and a complete wrist drop (A) does not occur. However, the PIN supplies the extensor digitorum communis, extensor indicis, extensor digiti minimi, and extensor pollicis longus. Consequently, injury to this nerve results in a characteristic "finger drop," which is an inability to extend the fingers and thumb at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints. Adduction of the fingers (D) is a function of the ulnar nerve. 2. Which cranial nerve is not contained within the superior orbital fissure? The contents include the oculomotor nerve (CN III), the trochlear nerve (CN IV), the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), and the abducens nerve (CN VI). It also transmits the superior ophthalmic vein. In contrast, the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery pass through a separate, more medially located foramen called the optic canal. Therefore, the optic nerve is not a content of the superior orbital fissure. This anatomical separation is a frequently tested point in neuroanatomy, distinguishing the pathways for vision from those controlling eye movement and sensation. 3. q1441.q: Which of the following is wrong about Ascaris lumbricoides?
o: Unembryonated fertilized egg takes time to infect after it goes in soil
q1441.ex: This question assesses knowledge of the giant roundworm, Ascaris lumbricoides. (A) Mostly asymptomatic : True. Light infections are very common and usually do not cause any noticeable symptoms. (B) Unembryonated egg needs time in soil : True. The fertilized eggs passed in feces are not immediately infective. During its life cycle, the ingested larvae penetrate the intestinal wall, travel to the lungs, and mature. This larval migration through the lungs can cause an eosinophilic pneumonitis known as Loeffler's syndrome, which presents with cough, wheezing, and dyspnea. (C) Heavy infection causes rectal prolapse : This statement is wrong. Rectal prolapse is a classic complication of heavy infection with the whipworm, Trichuris trichiura, not Ascaris. In individuals with sickle cell disease, this negatively charged, hydrophilic glutamic acid is replaced by the nonpolar, hydrophobic amino acid valine. This single change creates hemoglobin S (HbS), which has a tendency to polymerize under low-oxygen conditions, deforming the red blood cell into a rigid, sickle shape. q1463.q: Which of the following is seen in FFA (Fundus Fluorescein Angiography) in microaneurysm?
q1463.ex: Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) is a diagnostic procedure used to visualize retinal and choroidal circulation. Microaneurysms, which are saccular outpouchings of the retinal capillary walls, are often the earliest clinically detectable sign of diabetic retinopathy. During an FFA, fluorescein dye is injected intravenously and travels through the retinal vasculature. As the capillaries fill with dye during the arterial and early venous phases, the dye also fills these small, dilated sacs. Consequently, microaneurysms appear on the angiogram as small, discrete, well-demarcated points of increased brightness, which are best described as hyperfluorescent dots. In later phases of the angiogram, these microaneurysms may leak dye, leading to a more diffuse, hazy hyperfluorescence in the surrounding retina, indicative of macular edema. Hypofluorescence (B) would indicate a blockage of circulation, while hyperfluorescent lines or branching patterns (C, D) are more characteristic of neovascularization, a sign of advanced proliferative disease.

q1503.q: All of the following statements about Extrahepatic Biliary Atresia are true EXCEPT:
o: Kasai procedure should be done within 90 days
HIDA scan is used for diagnosis
Can be differentiated from other differential diagnoses by biopsy
Biliary atresia is the most common cause of neonatal cholestasis.
q1503.ex: Extrahepatic biliary atresia is a progressive inflammatory disease leading to fibrosis and obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts. It is the most common cause of pathological neonatal cholestasis (D) and the most common indication for pediatric liver transplantation. A hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan (B) is used to assess biliary excretion; failure of the tracer to reach the intestine is highly suggestive of the diagnosis. A liver biopsy (C) showing bile duct proliferation and portal tract fibrosis is often used for confirmation. The definitive surgical treatment is the Kasai procedure (hepatoportoenterostomy). The success of this procedure in restoring bile flow and preventing cirrhosis is highly time-dependent. It should be performed as early as possible, ideally before 60 days of life. The success rate drops significantly after 90 days. Therefore, the statement that it should be done within 90 days (A) is not ideal; it should be done much earlier. It is the "least true" statement.

q1532.q: Difficulty standing on one leg is caused by weakness of which muscle on the opposite (supporting) side?
q1532.ex: This question describes the biomechanics underlying the Trendelenburg sign. During the normal gait cycle, when a person lifts one leg off the ground to swing it forward, the pelvis on that unsupported side is prevented from dropping by the contraction of the hip abductor muscles on the contralateral, weight-bearing (supporting) side. q2077.q: Arrange the following structures in the correct order as they participate in the direct pathway of the basal ganglia : 1 Striatum 2 Globus pallidus 3 Substantia nigra 4 Thalamus 5 Cortex
q2077.ex: The direct pathway of the basal ganglia is a crucial circuit that facilitates the initiation of voluntary movement. The sequence begins with excitatory glutamatergic signals from the cerebral cortex (5) to the striatum (1) (caudate and putamen). The striatum then sends inhibitory GABAergic projections directly to the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi) and the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) (2 & 3). This inhibitory signal from the striatum suppresses the tonic inhibitory output of the GPi/SNr complex. The GPi/SNr normally inhibits the thalamus (4). By inhibiting the GPi/SNr, the striatum effectively disinhibits the thalamus, allowing it to send excitatory signals back to the motor cortex, thus promoting movement. Therefore, the correct sequence of information flow in the direct pathway is Cortex → Striatum → Globus Pallidus Internus/Substantia Nigra Pars Reticulata → Thalamus → Cortex. q2078.q: What is the typical prostate volume in adult males with normal health?
q2078.ex: The prostate is a gland in the male reproductive system located just below the bladder. In a healthy young adult male, the prostate is roughly the size of a walnut. Its volume is typically measured in cubic centimeters (cc) or milliliters (mL), which are equivalent units. The normal prostate volume is approximately 20 cc (or 20 grams). With age, the prostate often undergoes benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), which causes an increase in its size. Volumes of 50 cc, 75 cc, or 100 cc are indicative of significant prostatic enlargement, commonly seen in older men with BPH, and can lead to lower urinary tract symptoms due to compression of the urethra. Therefore, for an adult male in normal health without pathology, 20 cc represents the typical prostate volume. This standard value is important for diagnosing and staging conditions like BPH and prostate cancer. 9. q2090.q: In the instrument shown for determining hemoglobin levels, hemoglobin is converted into which of the following forms?
q2090.ex: The instrument shown is Sahli's haemoglobinometer, which is used for the colorimetric estimation of hemoglobin concentration in the blood. This method, also known as the acid hematin method, involves mixing a blood sample with a weak acid, typically 0.1 N hydrochloric acid (HCl), in a graduated tube. The acid lyses the red blood cells, releasing hemoglobin. The globin portion of the hemoglobin is denatured, and the heme is oxidized from ferrous () to ferric () state, forming a brown-colored compound called acid hematin (hematin hydrochloride). Distilled water is then added drop by drop until the color of the solution in the tube matches the color of the standard brown glass comparator rods in the instrument. The hemoglobin concentration is then read directly from the calibrated scale on the tube. This method is simple but less accurate than modern automated methods.

q2127.q: Which of the following cytokines does not play a direct role in causing the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction?
q2127.ex: The Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction is an acute inflammatory response that occurs after initiation of antibiotic therapy for spirochetal infections such as syphilis. It is caused by the rapid destruction of spirochetes, leading to the release of lipoproteins and other inflammatory components into the circulation. These microbial products stimulate macrophages and other immune cells to release pro-inflammatory cytokines. The key cytokines directly involved in mediating the reaction are TNF-α, IL-6, and IFN-γ. TNF-α plays a central role in producing fever, hypotension, and systemic inflammatory symptoms. IL-6 contributes to fever and acute phase responses, while IFN-γ enhances macrophage activation and amplifies the inflammatory cascade. IL-8, on the other hand, is primarily a chemokine responsible for neutrophil chemotaxis. Although it participates in general inflammatory processes, it is not considered a principal mediator directly responsible for the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction. Therefore, IL-8 is the cytokine that does not play a direct role in causing this reaction. q2188.ex: Hemiballismus is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by involuntary, violent, flinging (ballistic) movements of the limbs on one side of the body. The resulting disinhibition of the thalamus causes excessive excitatory output to the motor cortex, producing the characteristic large-amplitude, involuntary movements of hemiballismus. q2653.q: Which of the following methods can be used for therapeutic drug monitoring in a patient?
q2653.ex: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is the clinical practice of measuring the plasma concentration of a specific drug to maintain it within a target therapeutic range. This is essential for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, such as certain antiepileptics (e.g., phenytoin), antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin), and immunosuppressants (e.g., tacrolimus). Several analytical techniques are used for this purpose. High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) is a powerful and widely used technique in clinical laboratories for TDM. It works by separating the components of a mixture (like plasma) based on their physicochemical properties, allowing for the precise and accurate quantification of the specific drug of interest. While immunoassays are also very common, HPLC is a gold-standard reference method for many drugs. Spectrophotometry (C) is less specific, and NMR (B) and flow cytometry (D) are not used for routine TDM.

q2667.q: Which disease has an almost 100% fatality rate once symptoms develop?
q2667.ex: Rabies is an acute progressive viral encephalitis transmitted to humans through the saliva of infected animals, typically via a bite. While the disease is preventable with timely post-exposure prophylaxis, once clinical signs and symptoms develop, the disease is almost invariably fatal. The case fatality rate for symptomatic rabies approaches 100%. There are only a very small number of documented survivors of clinical rabies in the entire history of modern medicine, most of whom were treated with an experimental and not reliably successful protocol. This makes rabies one of the most lethal infectious diseases known. In contrast, while Nipah virus infection (B) and Ebola virus disease (C) are also extremely dangerous and have very high case fatality rates (which can range from 40% to over 90% depending on the strain and outbreak), survival is possible with intensive supportive care. Measles (D) has a much lower mortality rate. q2682.ex: For mass chemoprophylaxis of anemia in a population, the ideal preparation should be effective, safe, inexpensive, widely available, and suitable for large-scale public health distribution. Ferrous sulphate fulfills these criteria and is the most commonly recommended iron preparation in national anemia control programs. Ferrous sulphate contains a high proportion of elemental iron, is cost-effective, and has well-established efficacy in preventing and treating iron deficiency anemia. It is included in government initiatives such as the Anemia Mukt Bharat strategy under the National Health Mission in India. The tablet form allows easy distribution in schools, antenatal clinics, and community health programs. q2705.q: Which of the following is not an objective test?
q2705.ex: Audiological tests can be classified as objective or subjective (behavioral). Objective tests do not require a behavioral response from the patient; they measure a physiological response. Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA) or ABR (A), Impedance Audiometry (including tympanometry and acoustic reflex testing) (C), and otoacoustic emissions are all objective tests. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) (B) is an objective imaging test used in ophthalmology, not audiology. In contrast, Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) is a subjective or behavioral test. It requires the patient to listen to tones of specific frequencies and intensities and provide a conscious response (e.g., by raising a hand or pressing a button) when they hear the tone. The results depend entirely on the patient's perception and cooperation, making it a subjective measure of hearing thresholds. q2717.q: A 35-year-old man with a history of peptic ulcer disease presents with 2 days of abdominal pain and obstipation. An erect abdominal X-ray is obtained (as shown). What should be the next step in management? a. USG abdomen b. IV fluids c. Exploratory laparotomy d. Keep the patient in observation
q2717.ex: This 35-year-old man has acute abdominal pain and obstruction, and the erect abdominal X-ray shows free air under the diaphragm, indicating pneumoperitoneum. In a patient with a history of peptic ulcer disease, this strongly suggests perforated peptic ulcer, which is a surgical emergency. Management steps: (a) USG abdomen – Imaging helps confirm free fluid and assess intra-abdominal pathology. However, once free air is seen on X-ray, diagnosis is usually clear. (b) IV fluids – Immediate resuscitation is essential. These patients are at risk of dehydration, sepsis, and shock. IV fluids, nasogastric decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and proton pump inhibitors should be started. (c) Exploratory laparotomy – This is the definitive management. A perforated peptic ulcer requires urgent surgical repair to prevent generalized peritonitis and septic shock. Observation alone is inappropriate because perforation is life-threatening and requires urgent intervention. Therefore, the correct next steps include investigation, resuscitation, and emergency surgery — option (A).

q2726.q: A 40-year-old female undergoes cholecystectomy and later develops postoperative abdominal pain. Which test is used to detect a bile leak?
q2726.ex: When a post-cholecystectomy bile leak is suspected, the most sensitive and specific functional imaging study to identify the leak is a HIDA scan (Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid scan), also known as cholescintigraphy. This is a nuclear medicine test where a radioactive tracer (e.g., technetium-99m labeled mebrofenin) is injected intravenously. The tracer is taken up by the hepatocytes and excreted into the biliary system, mimicking the flow of bile. The flow of the tracer is imaged over time with a gamma camera. In a patient with a bile leak, the scan will show the tracer flowing normally through the bile ducts but will also demonstrate the abnormal extravasation of the tracer from the biliary tree into the peritoneal cavity, confirming the presence, and often the location, of the leak. While MRCP (B) shows anatomy and ERCP (A) is therapeutic, HIDA is the best test to functionally demonstrate an active leak.

q999.q: Which of the following statements are true regarding the relative risk associated with Mendelian patterns of inheritance?
q999.ex: 1/4 autosomal recessive This question asks for the correct recurrence risk for an affected child in a typical Mendelian inheritance scenario. For an autosomal recessive disorder, an affected child (genotype aa) is most commonly born to two heterozygous carrier parents (genotype Aa). In such a cross (Aa x Aa), the probability for each pregnancy is as follows: a 1 in 4 chance of having an affected child (aa), a 2 in 4 (or 1/2) chance of having an unaffected carrier child (Aa), and a 1 in 4 chance of having an unaffected, non-carrier child (AA). Therefore, the risk of having another child affected with the same autosomal recessive condition is 1/4 or 25%. The other options are incorrect for standard Mendelian patterns.
